prompt: At 22 weeks, a 2.3-mm dark band is seen on one oblique four-chamber frame. The outer myocardial boundary is unclear. What is the best next step?
options: Report a confirmed effusion because the band exceeds 2 mm.
Reacquire optimized views and cine clips, identifying the full myocardial wall before measuring.
Exclude effusion if routine color Doppler shows no signal.
Use adult effusion grading to decide whether the finding is significant.
reasons: A threshold does not establish that the calipers measured fluid. Anatomy must be confirmed.
Confirm a separate external collection on adequate repeat views, then measure fluid only and document the context.
An absent signal cannot independently exclude fluid; settings, angle and motion affect detection.
Adult centimeter grading does not apply to fetal pericardial fluid.

prompt: Which stored measurement best supports a fetal pericardial-fluid assessment using the ISUOG screening convention?
options: An oblique distance including the hypoechoic myocardial wall.
The total distance across both sides of the heart.
A perpendicular fluid-only depth at end-systole, with the view and location documented.
A measurement taken only at maximal apparent depth, without recording the phase.
reasons: Including muscle overestimates the collection.
Measure the fluid space, not total cardiac width or combined bilateral depths.
This measures the correct tissue space in a documented, reproducible phase. The ISUOG normal-rim convention uses end-systole.
A large apparent measurement without phase or boundary documentation is difficult to interpret and compare.

prompt: A suspected external gap disappears when the transducer is re-angled, and the complete myocardial boundary becomes visible. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Recognize angle-dependent dropout and document the adequate repeat views; reassess for any true residual collection.
Continue to label effusion from the first frame.
Assume the fluid resolved within seconds.
Lower the gain until the gap reappears.
reasons: A technically dependent gap favors artifact. The repeat examination must still assess whether a separate real collection remains.
Do not privilege an inadequate frame over reproducible anatomy.
Changing image appearance with angle is not evidence of biological resolution.
Excessively low gain may erase tissue and manufacture the appearance of fluid.

prompt: A fluid collection tracks around a compressed fetal lung and is outside the cardiac pericardial contour on thoracic sweeps. How should it be characterized?
options: Physiologic pericardial fluid.
Myocardial dropout.
Skin edema alone.
Pleural effusion, with a survey for additional fluid compartments.
reasons: The collection occupies the pleural space rather than the pericardial space.
A reproducible extra-cardiac collection surrounding a lung is not a myocardial dropout band.
Skin edema is located in the body wall, not around a lung inside the chest.
Name the anatomic compartment and look for hydrops or other associated findings.

prompt: A distinct external fluid collection is reproducible on grayscale cine in two planes. Low-velocity color Doppler shows no signal. Which interpretation is best?
options: True effusion is excluded.
Retain the grayscale assessment; absence of color does not exclude fluid.
Increase color gain until a signal appears and use that as proof.
Diagnose infection because simple fluid should always show color.
reasons: The historical color technique was not established as a stand-alone exclusion test.
Color may support difficult cases, but its absence must be interpreted with anatomy and technical limitations.
Blooming or flash artifact can generate misleading signal and cannot prove fluid.
There is no such diagnostic link between absent color and infection.

prompt: A fetus has confirmed pericardial effusion and new free abdominal ascites. No skin edema is present. What should the sonographer communicate?
options: The effusion is still isolated because edema is absent.
Hydrops requires all four fluid compartments.
Two abnormal fluid compartments meet the hydrops definition and require prompt clinician assessment.
Only the larger collection needs to be reported.
reasons: Ascites is a second abnormal fluid compartment, so the finding is no longer isolated.
Hydrops does not require simultaneous involvement of every compartment.
Pericardial fluid plus ascites meets the two-compartment criterion. Communicate the change and complete the fetal assessment.
The presence and distribution of every abnormal compartment affect interpretation.

prompt: During an indicated anemia assessment, reproducible MCA-PSV is 1.65 MoM using appropriate technique. What is the best next action?
options: Promptly notify the responsible clinician for suspected anemia and specialist assessment; do not call Doppler a definitive hemoglobin result.
Reassure because the fetus has no ascites.
Diagnose the exact hemoglobin concentration from the MoM value.
Schedule routine follow-up without communicating the result.
reasons: A value above 1.5 MoM raises concern for severe anemia. Management may involve fetal blood sampling with transfusion capability or delivery, depending on the clinical setting.
Anemia can be present before hydrops develops.
MCA-PSV estimates anemia risk; it is not a direct blood count.
A concerning reproducible result needs prompt clinical review.

prompt: A pathologic effusion is confirmed and appears isolated. Prior cfDNA screening was low risk. Which handoff best reflects current SMFM guidance?
options: No genetic discussion is needed after low-risk cfDNA.
Tell the patient that a normal karyotype excludes every genetic disorder.
Tell the patient that one-third of isolated small effusions have a single-gene disorder.
Arrange clinician/genetic counseling about diagnostic CMA ± karyotype; low-risk cfDNA does not replace diagnostic testing.
reasons: cfDNA is screening for selected conditions and does not replace a diagnostic discussion after a pathologic effusion.
Karyotype cannot exclude all copy-number or single-gene conditions.
Yields from heterogeneous hydrops-spectrum cohorts cannot be transferred to isolated small effusions.
SMFM #75 recommends diagnostic testing for one or more pathologic fetal effusions. The clinician should explain options and limits.

prompt: A small effusion remains isolated after a reassuring workup, with normal function and no hydrops. Which message is most appropriate?
options: The outcome is guaranteed to be normal and no follow-up is needed.
Prognosis is generally very good and spontaneous resolution is common; serial follow-up checks for new findings.
The fetus requires drainage because fluid is present.
The mixed-cohort 89.9% figure is the exact chance of a normal outcome for this fetus.
reasons: Residual uncertainty and evolving abnormalities make an absolute guarantee inappropriate.
This reflects the favorable historical evidence while preserving the purpose of ongoing observation.
Stable isolated effusions do not automatically need an invasive procedure.
That cohort includes nonisolated PE and does not estimate this individual fetus’s residual risk.

prompt: At follow-up, the effusion has increased and ventricular function appears reduced. What is the best sonographer action?
options: Wait for the scheduled follow-up because effusions often resolve.
Recommend a fixed delivery week based only on fluid depth.
Document the change and promptly notify the responsible clinician for fetal cardiology/fetal-center assessment.
Recommend immediate pericardiocentesis without specialist assessment.
reasons: New functional compromise changes the risk profile and should not be ignored.
There is no universal size-only delivery rule.
Trend plus functional deterioration warrants prompt review. The specialist team determines therapy, surveillance and delivery planning.
Drainage is individualized at a fetal center; imaging change does not independently establish a procedural indication.
